classes.name: normal / no fault
descriptions: A healthy OTDR trace with gradual baseline attenuation and no unexpected localized event.
The backscatter profile remains smooth across distance without an abrupt step, anomalous peak, or premature end.
A non-fault condition: no excess localized attenuation and no unexpected Fresnel reflection are visible in the raw trace.
Unlike a splice, bend, connector fault, cut, or reflector, the trace contains no distinct event morphology beyond the expected baseline.
Normal fiber operation with a stable trace and no location requiring corrective action.

classes.name: fiber tapping
descriptions: A fiber-tapping event caused by localized coupling or intrusion that perturbs the OTDR backscatter trace.
The raw trace shows a localized disturbance or small attenuation change rather than a clean high reflection or complete termination.
Typically a weakly reflective or non-reflective localized event with moderate disruption around one distance bin.
Unlike a cut the trace continues beyond the event; unlike a strong reflector it lacks a dominant narrow Fresnel peak.
A suspicious localized trace change consistent with physical access or optical coupling to the fiber.

classes.name: bad splice
descriptions: A poor fiber splice producing localized excess insertion loss in an OTDR trace.
The trace exhibits an abrupt downward step followed by continued backscatter at a reduced level.
Usually a non-reflective loss event, though a small reflection may appear when the splice contains a gap or defect.
Compared with bending, the transition is generally sharper and more step-like; compared with a cut, backscatter continues afterward.
A localized splice-quality fault that should be inspected and potentially re-spliced.

classes.name: bending event
descriptions: A macro-bend or micro-bend causing localized attenuation without a strong reflective interface.
The raw OTDR profile shows a gradual or moderately broad reduction in backscatter followed by a lower continuing level.
This is predominantly a non-reflective loss event with a wider transition than a clean point splice.
Unlike a connector or reflector it lacks a sharp Fresnel peak; unlike a cut the trace remains visible beyond the bend.
A localized bend-related attenuation signature suggesting excessive curvature or mechanical stress.

classes.name: dirty connector
descriptions: A contaminated or poorly seated connector producing abnormal loss and irregular reflection.
The OTDR trace contains a connector-like peak or messy localized disturbance with a level change after the event.
A reflective event whose shape and associated attenuation are less clean than a normal PC or UPC connector.
Compared with a good connector it has excessive or irregular loss; compared with a strong reflector its peak is less dominant.
A connector fault consistent with contamination, damage, or poor mating that warrants cleaning and reseating.

classes.name: fiber cut
descriptions: A broken fiber causing an abrupt termination of the OTDR backscatter trace.
The trace shows a sudden large drop or end-of-trace at the break distance, often after a prominent reflection.
A severe terminal loss event that may be strongly reflective when the broken glass forms an air interface.
Unlike a reflector or connector, meaningful backscatter does not continue beyond the event location.
A complete fiber break requiring repair or replacement at the detected termination point.

classes.name: PC / UPC connector event
descriptions: A normal physical-contact connector event with small insertion loss and a controlled reflection.
The raw trace shows a narrow connector-like reflection at an expected point with continued backscatter afterward.
A clean reflective event with modest amplitude and limited associated attenuation.
Unlike a dirty connector the event is regular with low excess loss; unlike a strong reflector the peak is comparatively moderate.
An expected mated PC or UPC connector signature rather than a severe fiber fault.

classes.name: strong reflector
descriptions: A highly reflective localized interface producing a strong Fresnel peak in the OTDR trace.
The raw trace contains a dominant narrow upward spike at one location, with the trace generally continuing afterward.
A strong reflective event that may arise from an open connector, reflective component, or high-index discontinuity.
Unlike a fiber cut the signal need not terminate after the peak; unlike a normal connector the reflected peak is much stronger.
A pronounced reflector that should be matched to planned hardware or investigated as an unexpected open interface.
